notes.meaning: Forty-two people returned from Azmaveth, a town in the territory of Benjamin. This place was also known as Beth-azmaveth in other biblical records. Even small villages were remembered and counted as God brought his people home.

These three neighboring towns sent back a total of 743 men. Long before the exile, they had been towns belonging to the Gibeonites who had made peace with Joshua. They are counted together here because each settlement had relatively few returnees.

Ramah and Geba together had 621 men return to Judah. Both were well-known towns in the land of Benjamin near Jerusalem. Geba had once been set aside for the priests, and Ramah was famous as the home of the prophet Samuel.

Michmash sent 122 men back from Babylon. This was the rocky mountain town where King Saul and his son Jonathan had once fought against the Philistines. The returnees went back to reoccupy their ancestors' land.

A group of 223 men came back to Bethel and Ai. These ancient places were famous in the early stories of Abraham and Joshua. The people returned to rebuild their lives where their ancestors had first worshiped the Lord.

Fifty-two men from Nebo returned to Judah. This Nebo was a local town in Judah, not the mountain in Moab where Moses died. Even though their numbers were small, they gladly made the long journey home.

The family of Magbish numbered 156 returning members. Unlike most of the surrounding names, which belong to towns, this was likely the name of an ancestral family head. God kept track of each household that chose to leave exile.

This clan is called the other Elam to distinguish it from the family of Elam listed earlier. Curiously, both groups numbered exactly 1,254 people. God watched over this large family and restored them to their homeland.

Three hundred and twenty people returned from the family of Harim. This group was an ordinary family of Israelites, distinct from the priestly family of the same name. Their name means consecrated, or set apart for God.

A total of 725 men returned to Lod, Hadid, and Ono. These towns were located west of Jerusalem in the coastal plain within the tribal area of Benjamin. Their return showed that the Jewish people were resettling areas beyond the immediate hills of Jerusalem.

Three hundred and forty-five men came back to settle in Jericho. Jericho was the historic city down in the Jordan valley, near the place where Israel first entered the promised land. Descendants from this town later helped rebuild Jerusalem's broken walls.

Senaah was by far the largest single group in the list, with 3,630 people returning. This name probably referred to an inhabited district not far north of Jericho. Their large numbers made them a great help in rebuilding the community.

The record turns to the priests, who were set apart to offer sacrifices and lead worship. The family of Jedaiah belonged to the high priest's household and had 973 members return. King David had originally established twenty-four shifts of priests, but only four returned from Babylon.

Over a thousand priests returned from the family line of Immer. This was the sixteenth priestly group established in King David's day. Their large number ensured there would be enough trained leaders to offer sacrifices in the rebuilt temple.

Pashhur was the largest priestly family to return, numbering 1,247 men. An ancestor with this name had once mistreated the prophet Jeremiah, but God still preserved his family. They returned ready to take up sacred work in the new temple.

The family of Harim was the fourth priestly group, with 1,017 men returning. They belonged to the third division of priests established under King David. Together, the four returning priestly families made up roughly one tenth of the entire returning population.

Levites were members of the tribe of Levi chosen to assist the priests and care for the temple. Remarkably, only 74 Levites returned, representing just two family lines. While thousands of priests came back, very few Levites were willing to leave their settled lives in Babylon for hard work in Judah.

Temple singers had the special duty of leading worship through music and praise. Only 128 singers returned, and all of them belonged to the family of Asaph, the famous songwriter of King David's time. The other ancient guilds of temple musicians were missing from this first return.

Gatekeepers were guards assigned to protect the temple doors and keep out anything unholy. Six families returned, numbering 139 men in total. Several of these families had served as temple guards in Jerusalem before the Babylonian exile began.

These temple servants were workers given to help the Levites with daily physical tasks like carrying water and cutting wood. Many of them were descendants of the Gibeonites whom Joshua had assigned to serve God's house long ago. Even though their duties were humble, God gave them an honored place in his written record.

The list of temple servant families continues through nine more family names. These households willingly traveled hundreds of miles to do the manual labor needed at God's altar. Their dedication shows that every role in serving God's house is honorable and pleasing to him.
